analysis.title: China: PBOC Changes Policy Rate to Overnight Benchmark
key_insights: The PBOC moved its policy rate from the 7-day to the overnight reverse repo rate, effective 2 November. The overnight reverse repo rate is set at 1.25%, 15bp below the 7-day rate of 1.40%, confirming earlier media reports.

Overnight reverse repo operations will run every business day as fixed-rate, quantity tenders. 7-day reverse repo operations become fixed-quantity, multiple-price tenders, used mainly around tax-payment periods and month-ends, so the 7-day rate matters less for policy.

Temporary repos/reverse repos and repo facilities for foreign central bank-type institutions, previously priced as a spread to the 7-day rate, are re-anchored to the overnight reverse repo rate with spreads unchanged. This makes the overnight rate the new policy rate.

The interest rate corridor shifts from 1.15-1.65% to 1.0-1.5%, which is +/-25bp around the overnight reverse repo rate of 1.25% instead of around 1.4%. The change aligns the PBOC with the Fed and ECB, which use overnight benchmarks.

GS says the next step would be to speed up loan repricing against the interbank overnight rate (DR001), as Governor Pan suggested. Daily overnight injections let the PBOC add and withdraw liquidity without delay, whereas 7-day injections often left excess liquidity on later days.

GS says this is not a conventional 15bp policy rate cut, but all else equal it raises interbank liquidity and lowers yields across the bond curve. The timing is earlier than many participants, GS included, expected.

GS attributes the earlier timing to the Zhuhai Huafa credit flare-up, related mutual fund redemptions and continued equity market weakness. Stronger-than-expected Q3 GDP reduced the pressure to secure this year's growth target. Rates markets appear to have priced in part of the move since Governor Pan's 19 October speech.

Client conversations suggest investors expect the 7-day reverse repo rate to fall to 1.30-1.35%, an effective policy rate cut of 5-10bp. GS therefore sees a further policy rate cut as unlikely in the near term.
Rising domestic credit risk could raise the odds of an RRR cut. The PBOC may also use its newly launched Bond-Market Non-Bank-Financial-Institution Swap Facility (BNSP) to contain risk spillovers.
GS expects China government bond yields and swap rates to grind lower, given weak economic fundamentals and the policy framework transition.
